newsitem.title: JAPAN: FREESTYLE SKIING-WORLD CHAMPION BATTLES AGAINST VERTIGO.
newsitem.headline: FREESTYLE SKIING-WORLD CHAMPION BATTLES AGAINST VERTIGO.

text.p: In his former life, world aerials champion Trace Worthington launched himself off icy ramps to the height of multi-storey buildings, twisting and turning in the air above the world's most glamorous ski resorts.

Now he stands at the bottom of the Mount Iizuna slope in Japan, site of the world freestyle skiing championships, wondering if he can rebuild himself as a world-beater before the Nagano Winter Olympics next year.

Worthington has vertigo, an impaired ability to control balance and movements in the air. Officially, it is called "Lost Move Syndrome", a condition previously diagnosed in divers and trampolinists, which he likens to amnesia or "a failure of the sub-conscious."
"People say to me: Why don't you retire?" said Worthington, who won the combined at the last world championships two years ago in La Clusaz, France.
"I did retire from what I did before and what I was. And now it's a kind of new beginning for me."

The 27-year-old American said his problem began in late 1995 at a competition in Park City, Utah. On a jump he had been performing since the age of 18, he unexpectedly crashed facing backward up the hill.
For an aerialist, a finely tuned ability to sense one's position in the air is critical to safe landings -- and to pulling off manoeuvres that make crowds gasp.
Worthington, who had always taken that air sense for granted, struggled afterward on the World Cup circuit before finally pulling out to concentrate on recovery.
Last December, after months spent rebuilding basic jumping mechanics, he began his World Cup comeback, placing as high as fourth at La Plagne, France, before Christmas.
But the bouts of vertigo returned, and he decided to pull out of the Nagano world championships and the remainder of the World Cup circuit, still the seventh-ranked aerialist in the world.
"It's not a physical thing in the sense that I'm 100 percent healthy," he said. "But I don't want to jump at 80 percent or 90 percent, and I'm not 100 percent in jumping."
"It's like skiing on a knee injury," he said. "I need to let it heal first."
The world champion, who also won World Cup titles in aerials and combined in 1995, says he will return to the task of relearning the basic mechanical skills of his sport.
"I'm up to a double twisting triple right now," said Worthington, referring to a jump he first performed nine years ago. "I have to be patient and build my way up.
"I'm looking at (my past successes) as part of a past life, something that happened a long time ago," he said. "It's time to move on. It's lost."
What he wants most is to remaster aerials -- and himself -- in time for the Olympics next February.

With that goal in mind, he has used the world championships purely as mental preparation, picturing himself at the top of the course getting ready for his Olympic jumps, identifying markers to orient himself in the air, getting a feel for the Mount Iizuna slope.
"My fear isn't doing the stuff," he said. "My fear is losing it again. I don't even care about crashing. I care about losing it again and not being able to go to the Olympics."
